polymers-001.question: Which polymer is synthesized by condensation (step-growth) polymerization?
choices: Nylon 66
Polyethylene
Polystyrene
polymers-001.explanation: Nylon 66 is synthesized by condensation polymerization of hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid, with one molecule of water released each time an amide bond forms. Condensation polymerization is step-growth polymerization, in which reactions between functional groups proceed stepwise, and high molecular weight is reached only at very high conversion. Polyethylene and polystyrene are made by addition (chain-growth) polymerization, in which the double bonds of ethylene or styrene open and link one after another, with no by-products. PET (polyethylene terephthalate) is also made by condensation polymerization, from ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid. Note that having “ethylene” in the name does not necessarily mean addition polymerization.

polymers-002.question: Which is a characteristic of thermosetting resins?
choices: They soften and melt when heated and set again on cooling, so they can be remolded any number of times
Their molecular chains are crosslinked into a three-dimensional network, and once cured they do not melt when heated
Their molecular chains are linear without crosslinks, so even after curing they dissolve readily in solvents
polymers-002.explanation: In thermosetting resins such as epoxy and phenolic resins, the curing reaction chemically bonds (crosslinks) the molecular chains into a three-dimensional network. Once cured they do not melt when heated; at high temperature they decompose before they flow. They have excellent dimensional stability, heat resistance and solvent resistance, and are used as semiconductor encapsulants, printed circuit boards and the matrix of CFRP. Softening and melting on heating and being remoldable any number of times are characteristics of thermoplastics such as polyethylene and PET. Thermoplastics have linear or branched chains without crosslinks, and many dissolve in solvents. A drawback of thermosets is that they are difficult to recycle.

polymers-003.question: Which statement about the glass transition temperature Tg and melting point Tm of a crystalline (semicrystalline) polymer is correct?
choices: Tg is higher than Tm
Tg is the temperature at which chain motion in the amorphous regions freezes or is released, and it is lower than Tm
Tg is the temperature at which the crystalline regions melt, and amorphous polymers, which have no crystals, have no Tg
polymers-003.explanation: A crystalline polymer consists of crystalline and amorphous regions. Tg is the temperature at which segmental motion of the chains in the amorphous regions freezes or is released; below Tg the polymer is hard and glassy, above it rubbery. Tm is the temperature at which the crystalline regions melt; Tg is always lower than Tm, and for many polymers Tg/Tm (as a ratio of absolute temperatures) is about 0.5–0.8. PET, for example, has a Tg of about 70–80 °C and a Tm of about 260 °C. It is Tm that represents melting of the crystalline regions; amorphous polymers such as polystyrene have no Tm, but they do have a Tg. Polymers such as polyethylene, whose Tg is below room temperature, are flexible because their amorphous regions are rubbery at room temperature.

polymers-004.question: A polymer sample consists of equal masses of molecules with a molecular weight of 1.0×10⁴ g/mol and molecules of 1.0×10⁵ g/mol. Which correctly gives the number-average molecular weight Mn and the weight-average molecular weight Mw?
polymers-004.explanation: With equal masses w of each, the number of molecules is proportional to the mass divided by the molecular weight. The number-average molecular weight is Mn = total mass/total number of molecules = 2/(1/1.0×10⁴ + 1/1.0×10⁵) ≈ 1.8×10⁴ g/mol. The weight-average molecular weight is the average weighted by mass fraction, Mw = 0.5 × 1.0×10⁴ + 0.5 × 1.0×10⁵ = 5.5×10⁴ g/mol. By number there are ten times as many small molecules, so Mn is pulled toward the small side, and Mw ≥ Mn always holds. The pair with Mn and Mw swapped has the order reversed, and the pair with both as a simple average ignores the difference between weighting by number and by mass. The dispersity Mw/Mn ≈ 3.0 is a measure of the breadth of the molecular weight distribution.

polymers-005.question: Take the density of perfectly crystalline polyethylene as 1.000 g/cm³ and that of fully amorphous polyethylene as 0.850 g/cm³. Which value is closest to the crystallinity (mass fraction) of a sample with a density of 0.925 g/cm³?
choices: About 46%
About 50%
About 54%
polymers-005.explanation: Assuming the volumes of the crystalline and amorphous regions are additive, the crystallinity by mass is Xc = ρc(ρs − ρa)/[ρs(ρc − ρa)] = 1.000 × (0.925 − 0.850)/[0.925 × (1.000 − 0.850)] = 0.075/0.13875 ≈ 0.54, about 54%. About 50% is the volume fraction obtained from (ρs − ρa)/(ρc − ρa), which differs from the mass fraction by the ratio of densities. About 46% is the mass fraction of the amorphous regions (1 − 0.54). The density method is a simple way to measure crystallinity; it can also be obtained from the heat of fusion by DSC or the ratio of crystalline peak areas in X-ray diffraction. The density of the perfect crystal can be calculated from the lattice parameters of the crystal structure.

polymers-006.question: For the same type of polymer, what generally happens as the crystallinity increases?
choices: Density and modulus increase, and transparency decreases
Density decreases and modulus increases
Density and modulus both decrease, and transparency increases
polymers-006.explanation: In crystalline regions the chains are packed regularly and densely, so higher crystallinity raises the density and strengthens interchain interactions, improving modulus, yield strength, heat resistance and chemical resistance. This is why high-density polyethylene (HDPE) is stiffer than low-density polyethylene (LDPE). On the other hand, crystalline and amorphous regions differ in refractive index, and spherulites and other features comparable to or larger than the wavelength of light scatter it, so transparency falls and the material turns milky. Gases also pass through crystalline regions with difficulty, so gas permeability decreases. A decrease in density is the opposite of what happens, and high transparency is characteristic of amorphous polymers such as PMMA and polycarbonate.

polymers-007.question: When a plasticizer is added to poly(vinyl chloride) (PVC), what happens to the glass transition temperature Tg and the properties of the material?
choices: Tg rises and the material becomes hard and brittle at room temperature
Tg falls and the material becomes soft at room temperature
Tg is unchanged and only the melting point of the crystals falls
polymers-007.explanation: A plasticizer works its way between the chains, weakening interchain interactions and increasing free volume, so segmental motion becomes easier and Tg falls. Rigid PVC has a Tg of about 80 °C, but adding plasticizer brings Tg below room temperature, giving the flexible PVC used for hoses and wire insulation. Raising Tg to make a polymer harder is done by introducing crosslinks or stiff aromatic rings, or by increasing the molecular weight. PVC has low crystallinity, and the plasticizer acts mainly by lowering the Tg of the amorphous regions, so it is not that only the melting point falls. When the plasticizer migrates to the surface over time, the material hardens or stains its surroundings.

polymers-008.question: Which statement about mechanical models of viscoelasticity is correct?
choices: The Maxwell model, a spring and dashpot in series, can represent stress relaxation under constant strain
The Voigt model, a spring and dashpot in parallel, can describe stress relaxation under constant strain
The Maxwell model can represent creep in which strain approaches a constant value under constant stress
polymers-008.explanation: When a constant strain is applied to the Maxwell model (series), the spring stretches first and stress develops; then the dashpot slowly extends while the spring contracts, so the stress relaxes as σ = σ₀exp(−t/τ) (τ = η/E). In the Voigt (Kelvin–Voigt) model (parallel), the spring and dashpot always have the same strain, so the stress does not relax under constant strain. What the Voigt model represents is delayed elasticity (creep), in which strain approaches a constant value over time under constant stress. Under constant stress, the strain of the Maxwell model does not approach a constant value but keeps increasing in proportion to time. Real polymers are approximated by combinations such as the four-element model.

polymers-009.question: A constant strain is applied to a polymer that can be represented by the Maxwell model, and the initial stress is 5.0 MPa. If the relaxation time is 50 s, which value is closest to the stress after 100 s?
choices: About 1.8 MPa
About 0.68 MPa
About 4.3 MPa
polymers-009.explanation: Stress relaxation in the Maxwell model follows σ(t) = σ₀exp(−t/τ), and t/τ = 100/50 = 2.0, so σ = 5.0 × exp(−2.0) = 5.0 × 0.135 ≈ 0.68 MPa. About 1.8 MPa uses exp(−1), the stress at t = τ. About 4.3 MPa is 5.0 × (1 − exp(−2)), confusing relaxation with an expression that grows over time, like creep in the Voigt model. The relaxation time is the ratio of viscosity to modulus, τ = η/E, and it shortens as temperature rises. The loss of clamping force in plastic gaskets and plastic parts in bolted joints is due to this stress relaxation.

polymers-010.question: A composite contains carbon fibers (Young's modulus 230 GPa) aligned in one direction in an epoxy resin (Young's modulus 3.5 GPa) at a volume fraction of 60%. Using the rule of mixtures, which value is closest to the Young's modulus in the fiber direction?
choices: About 8.6 GPa
About 94 GPa
About 139 GPa
polymers-010.explanation: When load is applied along the fibers, fiber and resin strain by the same amount (isostrain), so the modulus is the volume-fraction-weighted average E = VfEf + VmEm = 0.6 × 230 + 0.4 × 3.5 = 138 + 1.4 ≈ 139 GPa. About 94 GPa swaps the volume fractions of fiber and resin. About 8.6 GPa comes from the isostress expression 1/E = Vf/Ef + Vm/Em, which estimates the modulus perpendicular to the fibers. Because unidirectional material differs in stiffness by more than a factor of ten depending on direction, real components stack plies with different fiber orientations.

polymers-011.question: Which correctly describes the idea of time–temperature superposition in polymer viscoelasticity?
choices: Raising the temperature has the same effect as measuring over longer times (lower frequencies)
Raising the temperature has the same effect as measuring faster, over shorter times (higher frequencies)
Viscoelastic properties depend only on temperature, so changing the time scale or frequency of the measurement leaves the modulus unchanged
polymers-011.explanation: Molecular motion in polymers is faster at higher temperatures, so relaxations that occur in a short time at high temperature take a long time at low temperature. Relaxation modulus curves measured at different temperatures can therefore be shifted along a logarithmic time axis to overlap into a single composite curve (the master curve). In other words, raising the temperature has the same effect as measuring at longer times (lower frequencies). The amount of shift (the shift factor) is described by the WLF equation near Tg and by an Arrhenius-type expression well below Tg. Using this principle, long-term creep and stress relaxation at room temperature can be predicted from short tests at high temperature.

polymers-012.question: A composite consists of carbon fibers with a diameter of 7.0 µm and a tensile strength of 3.5 GPa in a resin whose fiber–matrix interfacial shear strength is 50 MPa. Which value is closest to the critical fiber length lc = σf·d/(2τc) needed to make full use of the fiber strength?
choices: About 0.12 mm
About 0.49 mm
About 0.25 mm
polymers-012.explanation: The critical fiber length is the length needed for stress transferred by interfacial shear from the fiber ends to reach the tensile strength at the middle of the fiber. lc = σf·d/(2τc) = 3.5×10⁹ × 7.0×10⁻⁶ / (2 × 50×10⁶) = 2.45×10⁻⁴ m, about 0.25 mm. About 0.49 mm forgets the 2 in the denominator, and about 0.12 mm uses the radius instead of the diameter. Fibers much longer than lc give reinforcement close to that of continuous fibers, while fibers shorter than lc pull out of the resin before they break. This is why fiber shortening from breakage during molding is a concern in injection-molded short-fiber-reinforced plastics.

polymers-013.question: In condensation polymerization between bifunctional monomers, assume the number-average degree of polymerization Xn and the extent of reaction p of the functional groups are related by the Carothers equation Xn = 1/(1 − p). What extent of reaction is needed to reach Xn = 200?
polymers-013.explanation: Solving Xn = 1/(1 − p) for p gives p = 1 − 1/Xn; for Xn = 200, p = 1 − 1/200 = 0.995, so 99.5% of the functional groups must react. At 95%, Xn is only 1/0.05 = 20, and 99.95% corresponds to Xn = 2000. Even at 90% conversion the degree of polymerization is only 10, so obtaining a high-molecular-weight polymer with useful strength by condensation polymerization requires driving the reaction almost to completion. This makes it essential to match the amounts of the two monomers precisely (for nylon 66, a salt of the diamine and the dicarboxylic acid is made to fix the 1:1 ratio) and to remove by-products such as water to shift the equilibrium toward the product.

polymers-014.question: Which correctly describes the relation between the stereoregularity (tacticity) of polypropylene and its properties?
choices: Atactic polypropylene, with randomly oriented methyl groups, packs its chains more densely and so reaches a higher crystallinity than isotactic
Stereoregularity is set by molecular weight alone, so samples of the same molecular weight have the same crystallinity and melting point regardless of tacticity
Isotactic polypropylene, with all methyl groups on one side, crystallizes and is stiff, while atactic, with random orientations, barely crystallizes
polymers-014.explanation: Every other carbon on the polypropylene backbone carries a methyl group, and the regularity of their orientation is called stereoregularity. In isotactic polypropylene, with all methyl groups on the same side, the chains can pack regularly as helices, so it crystallizes and becomes a stiff material with a melting point of about 160°C. Most commercial polypropylene is isotactic, made with catalysts such as Ziegler-Natta catalysts. In atactic polypropylene, with random orientations, the chains cannot pack regularly, so it hardly crystallizes and is a soft, tacky material. The statement that irregular chains pack more densely is the reverse of the truth. Stereoregularity is set by the polymerization catalyst and is a separate property from molecular weight. Atactic polystyrene is amorphous and transparent for the same reason.

polymers-015.question: A weight is hung from a strip of crosslinked rubber, stretching it to about twice its original length, and the temperature is then raised. Which combination of change in length and reason is correct?
choices: It lengthens, because, as in metals, the interatomic bonds weaken with temperature, the elastic modulus falls, and the load stretches it more easily
It shortens, because the elastic force comes from the entropic tendency of the chains to coil and grows in proportion to absolute temperature
It does not change, because the modulus of rubber is set only by the number of crosslinks and does not depend on temperature
polymers-015.explanation: Stretching rubber extends the coiled molecular chains, reducing the number of shapes they can take and lowering their entropy. Most of the elastic force of rubber comes from the tendency of the chains to return to the coiled state and increase their entropy, so it is called entropy elasticity. In the theory of rubber elasticity the modulus is proportional to the product of the crosslink density and the absolute temperature, so raising the temperature under a constant load strengthens the elastic force and the rubber shortens (the Gough-Joule effect). This is the opposite of the elasticity of metals (energy elasticity), which soften as the temperature rises. The modulus is proportional to temperature as well as to the number of crosslinks, so the statement that nothing changes is also wrong. At small extensions of about 10% or less, however, thermal expansion can dominate and the rubber lengthens.

polymers-016.question: A poly(vinyl chloride) sample (repeat unit −CH₂−CHCl−) has a number-average molecular weight of 1.25×10⁵ g/mol and a weight-average molecular weight of 2.25×10⁵ g/mol. Which is closest to its number-average degree of polymerization? Take the atomic masses as C 12.01, H 1.008 and Cl 35.45.
choices: About 3.6×10³
About 2.0×10³
About 4.6×10³
polymers-016.explanation: The repeat unit C₂H₃Cl has a mass of 2 × 12.01 + 3 × 1.008 + 35.45 ≈ 62.49 g/mol. The number-average degree of polymerization is the number-average molecular weight divided by this value: 1.25×10⁵/62.49 ≈ 2.0×10³. About 3.6×10³ divides the weight-average molecular weight and corresponds to the weight-average degree of polymerization. About 4.6×10³ leaves out the Cl and divides by C₂H₃ (27.04 g/mol). The broader the molecular weight distribution, the more the degree of polymerization depends on which average is used; this sample has Mw/Mn = 1.8.

polymers-017.question: Which statement about vulcanization, in which natural rubber is heated with sulfur, is correct?
choices: It cuts the chains to lower the molecular weight, softening the rubber so that it is easier to shape
Sulfur enters between the chains as a plasticizer and lowers the glass transition temperature
Sulfur bridges crosslink the chains, stopping flow and giving the material rubber elasticity
polymers-017.explanation: In unvulcanized raw rubber the chains are only entangled, so under sustained tension they slip past one another and flow, leaving permanent deformation. Heating with sulfur forms sulfur bridges (crosslinks) near the double bonds of the main chains, creating a three-dimensional network from which the chains cannot escape, so the rubber returns to shape even after large extensions. Too many crosslinks make it hard, and rubber with tens of percent of sulfur becomes hard ebonite. Cutting the chains to soften the rubber is mastication, done before vulcanization, and lowering Tg as a plasticizer does is not the purpose of vulcanization either.

polymers-018.question: SBS (a polystyrene-polybutadiene-polystyrene block copolymer) can be used as a rubber at room temperature without vulcanization and can be reshaped by heating. What is the correct reason?
choices: Hard glassy domains formed by the polystyrene end blocks act as physical crosslinks that soften on heating
Styrene and butadiene alternate and crystallize, and the crystals act as chemical crosslinks that do not melt at room temperature
The heat of molding makes the polystyrene blocks bond chemically, giving the same network as a thermoset
polymers-018.explanation: In SBS the polystyrene end blocks (Tg about 100°C) and the central polybutadiene block (Tg far below room temperature) do not mix and separate into nanometer-scale domains. At room temperature the hard, glassy polystyrene domains anchor the ends of the rubbery polybutadiene chains and act as physical crosslinks, so the material behaves elastically like vulcanized rubber. Heated above their Tg the domains soften and flow, so the material can be reshaped like a thermoplastic. This is a thermoplastic elastomer. It involves neither alternating crystals nor chemical crosslinks.

polymers-019.question: The glass transition temperature of an amorphous polymer follows the Flory-Fox equation Tg = Tg∞ − K/Mn, with Tg∞ = 100°C (the value for very high molecular weight) and K = 1.0×10⁵ K·g/mol. Which is closest to Tg for a sample with a number-average molecular weight Mn = 5.0×10³ g/mol?
choices: About 120°C
About 100°C
About 80°C
polymers-019.explanation: K/Mn = 1.0×10⁵/5.0×10³ = 20 K, so Tg = 100 − 20 = 80°C (a temperature difference has the same value in K and °C). Chain ends move more easily than the middle of a chain and carry more free volume, so samples with lower molecular weight, and hence more chain ends, have a lower Tg. About 120°C adds K/Mn, a sign error. About 100°C ignores the effect of molecular weight and holds only for very large Mn. With this equation, K/Mn falls to about 1 K at Mn around 10⁵ g/mol, and beyond that Tg is almost constant.

polymers-020.question: When a glassy amorphous polymer such as polystyrene or PMMA is pulled at room temperature, crazes may form before fracture. Which statement about crazes is correct?
choices: They are thin bands of crystal with regularly aligned chains, elongated parallel to the tensile stress
They spread perpendicular to the tensile stress, and their interior consists of fine fibrils and voids
They are shear bands in which chains slide without a change in volume, containing no voids at all
polymers-020.explanation: A craze is a thin region that spreads along a plane perpendicular to the tensile stress; inside it, bundles of drawn chains form fibrils bridging the two faces, surrounded by voids. Unlike a crack it can carry some load, but when the fibrils break it becomes a crack and starts brittle fracture. Crazes scatter light and cause the stress whitening seen at bends. Chains sliding without a volume change form shear bands, a different mode of deformation, and crazes are not crystalline bands either. High-impact polystyrene (HIPS) absorbs impact energy by having rubber particles initiate many crazes.

polymers-021.question: Which statement correctly compares how molecular weight changes during the reaction in radical (chain-growth) polymerization of styrene and in condensation (step-growth) polymerization such as that of nylon 66?
choices: Radical polymerization gives high-molecular-weight chains from the start, coexisting with monomer; in condensation polymerization molecular weight stays low until conversion is high
In radical polymerization dimers and trimers form first and molecular weight becomes large only near the end; in condensation polymerization it is high from the start
In both, every molecule grows a little at a time at the same rate, so molecular weight increases in proportion to reaction time
polymers-021.explanation: In radical polymerization, monomers add one after another to radicals generated from an initiator; each chain grows to a degree of polymerization of thousands or more within a very short time and then stops growing by termination. From the start of the reaction, therefore, the mixture contains high-molecular-weight chains and unreacted monomer, and as the reaction proceeds mainly the amount of polymer increases. In condensation polymerization any functional groups can react, so dimers and trimers form first and then join up; as the Carothers equation shows, molecular weight does not become large until conversion approaches 99%. Statements that swap the two behaviors are wrong, and in neither case does molecular weight grow in proportion to time.

polymers-022.question: Which statement correctly describes the crystal structure formed when polyethylene is crystallized by slow cooling from the melt?
choices: Each molecule stretches straight along its whole length, and needle-like crystals several micrometers or more long appear separately in the melt
Chains line up without folding anywhere and grow into a large single crystal, until in the end the whole sample becomes one crystal
Plate-like crystals (lamellae) about 10 nm thick, made of folded chains, grow radially from a center to form spherulites
polymers-022.explanation: Because the molecules are very long, on crystallizing from the melt the chains do not line up at full length but fold back and forth many times within thin plate-like crystals (lamellae) about 10 nm thick. The chain axis is roughly perpendicular to the lamellar surface. The lamellae grow radially from a nucleus, branching as they go, to form spherical aggregates (spherulites), and between the lamellae amorphous regions remain, made of chain portions that could not enter the crystal and tie chains linking several lamellae. The crystallinity of a crystalline polymer therefore never reaches 100%, and the structure is a mixture of crystalline and amorphous regions. Fully extended needle-like chains or a whole sample forming one single crystal are not the normal outcome of crystallization from the melt.

polymers-023.question: What happens when molded parts of nylon 6 or nylon 66 absorb water in a humid environment?
choices: Water reacts with the amide groups to form new crosslinks between chains, so the glass transition temperature rises and the part becomes hard and brittle
Water breaks into the hydrogen bonds of the amide groups and acts like a plasticizer, lowering Tg and modulus and slightly enlarging the part
Nylon consists only of hydrocarbon, so it absorbs almost no water, and its dimensions and properties do not change with humidity
polymers-023.explanation: Nylon chains carry highly polar amide groups (−CO−NH−), and neighboring chains attract each other through hydrogen bonds. Water molecules form hydrogen bonds with the amide groups and slip between the chains, weakening the attraction between them, so like a plasticizer they lower the glass transition temperature. As a result, modulus and strength fall compared with the dry state, impact resistance improves, and the volume grows so that dimensions change. Design of nylon parts for dimensions and strength therefore assumes the water content reached at the service humidity. Water does not form crosslinks with the amide groups. Nylon contains nitrogen and oxygen in its main chain and, unlike all-hydrocarbon polyethylene, readily absorbs water.

polymers-024.question: The zero-shear viscosity η₀ of a polymer melt is proportional to the 3.4th power of the weight-average molecular weight in the range where chain entanglements act. By about what factor does η₀ change if the weight-average molecular weight is doubled at the same temperature?
choices: About 11 times
About 2 times
About 6.8 times
polymers-024.explanation: Since η₀ ∝ Mw^3.4, doubling the molecular weight multiplies η₀ by 2^3.4 ≈ 10.6, about 11 times. Longer chains take much more time to work their way out between the surrounding entangled chains (reptation-like motion), so viscosity rises steeply. About 2 times applies η₀ ∝ Mw, the relation for low molecular weights where entanglements do not act. About 6.8 times mistakes the 3.4th power for multiplying by 3.4, giving 2 × 3.4. Raising molecular weight improves strength and impact resistance but makes the melt flow less readily and complicates injection molding, so molecular weight is chosen to suit the application.

polymers-025.question: The temperature dependence of relaxation times in an amorphous polymer is described by the WLF equation log a_T = −17.44(T − Tg)/(51.6 + T − Tg), where a_T is the ratio to the relaxation time at Tg and temperatures are in K. A relaxation that takes one day (8.64×10⁴ s) at Tg takes about how long at 20 K above Tg?
choices: About 200 years
About 11 minutes
About 1.2 seconds
polymers-025.explanation: With T − Tg = 20 K, log a_T = −17.44 × 20/(51.6 + 20) = −348.8/71.6 ≈ −4.87, so a_T ≈ 1.34×10⁻⁵. The relaxation time is 8.64×10⁴ × 1.34×10⁻⁵ ≈ 1.2 s; just 20 K above Tg the relaxation runs about 70,000 times faster. About 11 minutes treats the base-10 logarithm as a natural logarithm and uses exp(−4.87). About 200 years divides by a_T, assuming relaxation slows at higher temperature, which is the wrong direction. Near Tg the rate of molecular motion changes extremely steeply with temperature, more steeply than an Arrhenius form. When the time-temperature superposition principle is used to predict long-term properties from short-time measurements, the WLF equation gives the amount of shift.

polymers-026.question: According to the theory of rubber elasticity, the shear modulus of a crosslinked rubber is G = ρRT/Mc (ρ is the density and Mc the molecular weight between crosslinks), and Young's modulus at small strains is E = 3G. For ρ = 950 kg/m³, Mc = 5000 g/mol and T = 300 K, which is closest to E? Take R = 8.314 J/(mol·K).
choices: About 1.4 MPa
About 0.47 MPa
About 1.4 kPa
polymers-026.explanation: Taking Mc as 5.0 kg/mol, G = 950 × 8.314 × 300/5.0 ≈ 4.7×10⁵ Pa = 0.47 MPa, and E = 3G ≈ 1.4 MPa. About 0.47 MPa takes G itself as E, and about 1.4 kPa leaves Mc as 5000 in g/mol without making the units consistent. The modulus rises as Mc becomes smaller (denser crosslinking) and as the temperature rises, which reflects the entropic nature of rubber elasticity. The value is about five orders of magnitude below the Young's modulus of metals (tens to hundreds of GPa), which corresponds to rubber stretching a lot under a small force.

polymers-027.question: Polystyrene has a glass transition temperature of about 100 °C, far higher than that of polyethylene (well below room temperature). Which is the main reason?
choices: Polystyrene is highly crystalline, and its hard crystals hold the chains of the amorphous regions in place up to above room temperature
Its bulky benzene-ring side groups hinder rotation about the backbone, so a higher temperature is needed before the chains can move
Polystyrene chains are crosslinked to one another by chemical bonds into a network, so they can hardly move even when heated
polymers-027.explanation: The glass transition is the temperature at which chains in the amorphous regions gain large-scale mobility through rotation about the backbone bonds. The polyethylene backbone is just a string of −CH₂− units that rotate easily, so its glass transition temperature is far below room temperature. Polystyrene carries a bulky benzene-ring side group on every repeat unit, which hinders backbone rotation and stiffens the chain, so the chains cannot move much until about 100 °C. Polycarbonate, with aromatic rings in the backbone itself, has an even higher value. Ordinary polystyrene is atactic and does not crystallize, and as a thermoplastic it is not crosslinked.

polymers-028.question: Which statement about gel permeation chromatography (GPC, size exclusion chromatography), used to measure the molecular weight distribution of polymers, is correct?
choices: Smaller molecules pass quickly through the pores of the packing and come out first, so the order of elution gives the distribution from low to high molecular weight
It ionizes the molecules one by one and weighs them, so molecular weights themselves are obtained directly and accurately without any standards
Molecules with larger coils in solution cannot enter the pores of the packing and come out first, so molecular weights are found by calibration with standards
polymers-028.explanation: In GPC a dilute polymer solution is passed through a column packed with porous gel particles. Molecules with large coils in solution cannot enter the pores and travel only between the particles, so they emerge early, while small molecules penetrate the pores, take a longer path and emerge later. What is separated is molecular size (the coil size in solution), so the relation between elution time and molecular weight is established with standards of known molecular weight, such as polystyrene, and used for conversion. For polymers of different structure the results are therefore relative values. Mn and Mw are calculated from this distribution. Ionizing molecules and weighing them is mass spectrometry, a different method from GPC.

polymers-029.question: When an amorphous polymer such as PC or PMMA is kept for a long time below its glass transition temperature, it gradually becomes stiffer and more brittle and creeps less, even without any chemical change (physical aging). Which is the reason?
choices: The excess free volume frozen in on cooling decreases through slow molecular motion, approaching the denser packing of equilibrium
Oxygen in the air slowly cuts the chains and lowers the molecular weight, so entanglements decrease and the polymer becomes stiff and brittle
Chains in the amorphous regions line up over time, raising the crystallinity and increasing the fraction of hard crystals
polymers-029.explanation: A glass formed by cooling through the glass transition is a non-equilibrium state in which the packing of the liquid was frozen partway, so it holds more free volume than at equilibrium. Even below the glass transition temperature the chains can still move slightly, so over long times the volume shrinks toward the denser equilibrium packing. As a result the modulus and yield stress rise, the material becomes more sensitive to impact, and creep and stress relaxation slow down. Because no chemical bonds change, heating above the glass transition temperature restores the original state. Chain scission by oxygen is chemical degradation and is not reversed by heating. Changes in an amorphous polymer that does not crystallize cannot be explained by increasing crystallinity.

polymers-030.question: A chain with N = 1.0×10⁴ backbone bonds of length l = 0.154 nm is treated as a freely jointed chain, in which the bond directions are independent of one another. Which is closest to the root-mean-square end-to-end distance √N·l?
choices: About 1.5 µm
About 15 nm
About 1.5 nm
polymers-030.explanation: √N = √(1.0×10⁴) = 100, so √N·l = 100 × 0.154 nm ≈ 15 nm. About 1.5 µm is the length of the chain stretched straight (the contour length), N·l = 1540 nm; a real chain coils up like a ball of yarn, and its end-to-end distance is only about one-hundredth of the contour length. About 1.5 nm takes √N as 10 by mistake. In real chains, fixed bond angles and restricted rotation make the coil about two to three times larger than a freely jointed chain, but it still scales with √N. When rubber is stretched, these coiled chains are extended, and the entropic tendency to return to the coiled state is the source of its elasticity.
